analysis.one_liner: Bans employment contracts that silence workers about workplace harassment and ends tax deductions for harassment settlement costs.
analysis.headline: The EMPOWER Act, which had 89 cosponsors including 4 Republicans, never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to require workers to sign nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreements that cover workplace harassment, and illegal to enforce such clauses. It would preserve every worker's right to report harassment to the EEOC, state agencies, police, and the courts, no matter what they signed. It would also require public companies to disclose how many harassment settlements they pay and how much, and it would end the tax deduction companies take for harassment judgments, legal fees, and liability insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, applicants, interns, temp workers, and independent contractors who experience or witness harassment. They could no longer be forced to sign away their ability to speak about or report harassment as a condition of getting or keeping a job, and harassment victims would no longer owe income tax on settlement money.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to require, as a condition of hiring, promotion, pay, or benefits, a contract containing a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause covering workplace harassment, and makes it unlawful to enforce such a clause.
States that employees and applicants keep all rights to report harassment to the EEOC, federal and state agencies, law enforcement, and the courts, regardless of any clause they have signed.

Requires the EEOC to set up a confidential tip-line that supplements the formal discrimination-charge process, flag patterns of complaints against the same employer, and develop workplace harassment training and public education.

Requires public companies to disclose in annual 10-K filings the number of harassment settlements and judgments against them, the total amounts paid, and patterns of multiple settlements tied to the same individual.

Ends corporate tax deductions for amounts paid under harassment judgments, related litigation expenses and attorney's fees, and insurance covering harassment liability, while excluding harassment settlement and judgment payments from victims' taxable income and allowing income averaging over the years the back pay covers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large companies — would lose the contractual ability to keep harassment confidential, would have to count and publish their harassment settlements in SEC filings, and would pay tax on settlement and litigation costs they currently deduct. The EEOC and state fair-employment agencies would bear new administrative work.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves a large carve-out: nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses are still allowed in settlement and separation agreements that resolve pre-existing claims, so a worker who settles a harassment claim after the fact can still be silenced — the secrecy pipeline that hid most cases would largely remain open.
The EEOC tip-line and training provisions only take effect if Congress appropriates at least $1,000,000–$1,500,000 per year, so the reporting channel could simply never be funded.
The tip-line does not allow anonymous reporting and its reports would not by themselves trigger individual investigations, so it supplements rather than replaces the formal charge process.

Denying deductions for harassment judgments, legal costs, and related insurance raises the after-tax cost of settlements for employers, a real cost that defenders of the bill would have to acknowledge, and public companies would carry new compliance burdens on their SEC filings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — that no one can be required to sign away their right to speak about or report harassment as a condition of a job — is significant and hard to object to in good faith, and it would extend to interns, temps, and contractors who today often fall outside employer policies. The honest costs are compliance and tax costs for employers, new reporting burdens for public companies, and a design limit: because negotiated settlements can still include confidentiality, the bill restrains the strongest silence tool (the condition-of-employment clause) while leaving the settlement NDA intact. The tax change is the most one-sided part: it makes harassment more expensive for employers, which is the stated goal, but it is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in April 2019, and never got a markup, a hearing, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Frankel introduced the EMPOWER Act in the House on March 5, 2019, with Rep. John Katko among the original cosponsors.
It gathered 88 cosponsors — 84 of 231 House Democrats and 4 of 197 House Republicans.
The House referred it to six committees: Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Financial Services, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Judiciary.
On April 8, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no further action was ever taken.
The bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without a committee or floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use harassment nondisclosure clauses kept that tool for new hires, and companies continued deducting harassment settlement and litigation costs from their taxes. Workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Lois Frankel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the EMPOWER Act and organized its cosponsorship.

for.name: Rep. John Katko
for.what_they_did: Put his name on the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan from day one.

against.name: Chairs of the six committees of referral
against.role: Chairs, Education and Labor; Ways and Means; Financial Services; House Administration; Oversight and Reform; Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill was moved to a subcommittee in April 2019 and never came back out before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 84 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored versus 4 of 197 House Republicans — and no recorded vote ever took place.

industries.note: The bill would bar employers from requiring harassment NDAs as a condition of employment and from enforcing them, and would deny tax deductions for harassment judgments, litigation costs, and liability insurance. Its main cost falls on companies that currently use silence clauses to keep harassment claims out of public view.

They would face new SEC disclosure requirements counting their harassment settlements and payments, which exposes reputational and financial information shareholders and the public currently cannot see.
They would gain a confidential tip-line, pattern-monitoring, and training responsibilities — but only if Congress appropriates the required funding each year.
